content: It is not appropriate to provide children in this age group with low-fat animal milk or plant-based milk substitutes as their primary source of nutrition. Evidence is required to establish adequate recommendations that ensure proper growth, health, and nutrition for young children during their second year of life, particularly within the critical first 1,000 days of development. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of animal milk consumption and its associated benefits or risks in children aged 12–23 months. This was compared to follow-on formula marketed for children over one year of age, lower-fat milk, plant-based milk alternatives, or fortified milk. Criteria for Study Inclusion: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with randomization at either the individual or cluster level, non-randomized controlled trials (e.g., allocation by birth date or alphabetical order), comparative observational studies with control groups, controlled cohort studies (prospective and retrospective), controlled before-and-after studies with at least two control and two intervention sites, and interrupted time series with at least three measurement points before and after the intervention. Types of Interventions: The interventions involved the consumption of various types of milk, including full-fat or lower-fat animal milk and milk substitutes, as part of the daily diet of young children. The comparisons included: 1. Animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) versus no other milk. 2. Animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) versus follow-on formula marketed for children over one year. 3. Full-fat animal milk versus lower-fat milk. 4. Animal milk (full-fat or lower-fat) versus plant-based milk alternatives. Outcomes: The outcomes were selected based on their relevance to the intervention and prioritized in consultation with the guideline development group (GDG). Seven critical outcomes were included in the evidence profile: 1. Growth (weight, height, head circumference, weight-for-age z-score, height-for-age z-score). 2. Body composition (percentage of body fat or as defined by trialists). 3. Long-term food preferences or dietary patterns (as defined by trialists). 4. Long-term outcomes related to non-communicable diseases (as defined by trialists). 5. Nutrient status (e.g., fatty acids, triglycerides, lipoproteins, micronutrient concentrations). 6. Child development (as defined by trialists). 7. Anemia (hemoglobin concentration below a defined cut-off, adjusted for altitude, or as defined by trialists), iron deficiency anemia (IDA), and iron deficiency (serum ferritin <12 µg/L or as defined by trialists). Important outcomes included: 1. Nutrient intakes (sufficient or excessive, as defined by trialists). 2. Feeding methods, eating habits, or use of feeding bottles/cups (as defined by trialists). 3. Oral health (e.g., dental caries). 4. Gastrointestinal health (e.g., diarrhea, gastroesophageal reflux, as defined by trialists). 5. Dietary diversity (proportion of children aged 12–23 months receiving foods from at least four food groups, as defined by UNICEF or trialists). 6. Gastrointestinal tolerance (e.g., regular bowel movements, discomfort, as defined by trialists). 7. Allergies (e.g., IgE-mediated gastrointestinal milk allergy, as defined by trialists). 8. Plasma concentrations of isoflavones (e.g., genistein, daidzein, as defined by trialists). Search Strategy: We searched for studies without restrictions up to September 2020 using databases such as PubMed, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and others. Secondary reference searching was conducted on included studies and related review articles. Experts in the field were contacted to identify unpublished articles and conference abstracts. Screening and Selection: All records were screened using Covidence systematic review software. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against selection criteria. Full-text reports of relevant studies were assessed for eligibility. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. Decisions were documented in a PRISMA diagram. Data Extraction and Management: Data from eligible studies were extracted using a detailed form. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. If information was unclear, study authors were contacted for clarification. Data collection forms recorded study identification, design, outcomes, and risk of bias assessments. Risk of Bias Assessment: The risk of bias in RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, considering factors such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources of bias. Observational studies were assessed using the ROBINS-I tool, which evaluates bias due to confounding, participant selection, intervention classification, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results. Data Analysis: Cluster-randomized studies were included alongside individually randomized studies, with adjustments for clustering effects. Multi-arm studies included only directly relevant arms. Random-effects meta-analyses were used to account for heterogeneity in interventions, populations, and methods. Dichotomous outcomes were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and continuous outcomes as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity and Reporting Bias: Heterogeneity was assessed using forest plots, I², and T² statistics. Substantial heterogeneity (I² > 50%) was noted and explored through subgroup analyses. Reporting biases were investigated using funnel plots and by contacting study authors for missing data. Certainty of Evidence: The GRADE approach was used to interpret findings. Evidence from RCTs was downgraded for serious limitations, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies started at low certainty. GRADE profiler software was used to create evidence profile tables. Subgroup Analysis: Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore differences between studies based on factors such as prevalence of conditions, type of feeding before 12 months, and funding sources. Sensitivity Analysis: Sensitivity analyses were performed to examine the effects of clustering, missing data, and study design on overall treatment effect estimates. Results: The search identified 4,065 references (4,033 after removing duplicates). After screening, 88 articles were reviewed in full text, and 19 studies (36 references) were included. Thirteen RCTs contributed to meta-analyses. The included studies involved 5,579 participants and were published between 1986 and 2018. Two studies were cluster-randomized, and adjustments for clustering effects were made in the analysis.
